This on-site session was a **pure recap session**: no new material was
introduced. Instead, we discussed the topics from the previous sessions that
you wanted to go through again. We focused on two of them: how to tell R where
your files are (absolute vs. relative paths and the `here` package), and the
different object types in R and how they relate to each other.

The new material of this week, Quarto and R Markdown, is covered in the
[videos of session 5](/content/material/s_05_Quarto.qmd).

## 📂 Absolute and relative paths, and the `here` package

We discussed the difference between **absolute paths** (starting at the root of
one specific computer) and **relative paths** (starting at the current working
directory), and why only paths built with the **`here` package** keep working
when your code moves to another computer, another folder, or another working
directory.

We went through parts of a small hands-on exercise. The repository contains
three scripts that read the same data file with an absolute path, a hard-coded
relative path, and `here`, respectively. Download it as a ZIP file and work
through the experiments described in its README:

[**Go to the exercise repository**](https://github.com/teaching-datascience/here-paths-demo){.btn .btn-primary}

The background is covered in Part III of the
[slides on project management](/content/material/s_03_ProjectManagement.qmd)
from session 3, and in the following reading:

- [Setting Up an R Project](https://euf-methodology-hub.netlify.app/resources/setting-up-an-r-project) on *Method and Inquiry* [@graebner2026-setting-up-an-r-project]

## Summary: the most important transformations

The table summarises section 8 of `ObjectHierarchy.R`. Read it row by row:
to transform an object of the type in the first column into the type in the
header, use the function in the cell.

| from ↓ \\ to → | logical | integer | double | character | list | factor | data.frame |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **logical** | — | `as.integer()` | `as.double()` | `as.character()` | `as.list()` | `factor()` | — |
| **integer** | `as.logical()` | — | `as.double()` | `as.character()` | `as.list()` | `factor()` | — |
| **double** | `as.logical()` | `as.integer()` | — | `as.character()` | `as.list()` | `factor()` | — |
| **character** | `as.logical()` | `as.integer()` | `as.double()` | — | `as.list()` | `factor()` | — |
| **list** | `unlist()` | `unlist()` | `unlist()` | `unlist()` | — | — | `as.data.frame()` |
| **factor** | — | `as.integer()`\* | — | `as.character()` | `as.list()` | — | — |
| **data.frame** | — | — | — | — | `as.list()` | — | — |

: \* gives the internal codes, not the labels; use `as.numeric(as.character(x))`
to get the values.

- **Upwards** in the atomic hierarchy (logical → integer → double →
  character) nothing gets lost.
- **Downwards**, values can be truncated (`as.integer(2.99)` is `2`) or become
  `NA` (`as.numeric("two")`).
- Always check the result with `typeof()` or `class()` after transforming an
  object.
:::

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Checklist: object types in practice

The checklist at the end of `ObjectTypesInPractice.R`; go through it every
time you work with a new data set.

- [ ] After reading in data, check the types with `typeof()`, `class()` or
  `str()`.
- [ ] Variables you calculate with should be **numeric** (integer or double).
- [ ] Identifiers (IDs, postal codes, phone numbers) should stay
  **character**.
- [ ] Yes/no variables are most convenient as **logical**: `sum()` gives you
  a count, `mean()` a share.
- [ ] Categories with a fixed set of values should be **factors**; ordered
  categories should be **ordered factors** with the levels in the right order.
- [ ] If `as.*()` returns `NA`s with a warning, find out which values caused
  them.
- [ ] Never transform a factor directly into a number; go via
  `as.character()` first.
:::
